record.question:
An education company runs application servers on EC2 and in its data center. Each server writes structured JSON logs with a level field. Operations needs an alert within minutes when an error-count metric reaches at least 20 during a five-minute period. Log delivery is prompt and monitored. The company wants centralized logs and minimal custom processing code.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Collect logs with the CloudWatch agent and run an hourly Logs Insights query that sends an SNS notification when the previous hour contains errors.
Collect host CPU metrics with the CloudWatch agent and notify an SNS topic when average CPU utilization exceeds 80 percent.
Collect logs in CloudWatch Logs and write a subscription Lambda function to parse errors, maintain counts, publish a custom metric, and trigger an SNS-backed alarm.
Collect logs in a Standard CloudWatch Logs log group with the CloudWatch agent. Use a metric filter for ERROR events and an alarm on a five-minute Sum of at least 20, with an SNS action.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. The agent centralizes both sets of logs. A filter that matches the structured level field and contributes a value of 1 converts matching events into an error-count metric. The alarm evaluates the Sum over the specified period and sends the configured SNS notification when it enters ALARM.

<<1>> retains centralized logs but its hourly schedule cannot meet the requested notification latency.

<<2>> measures resource utilization, not application errors. Error counts can rise while CPU remains low, or CPU can rise without an error.

<<3>> can implement the behavior, but adds parsing, aggregation, and publishing code that a native metric filter avoids for this simple predicate.

Use a Standard log group because metric filters are not supported in every log class. Filters apply to newly ingested events and do not backfill historical logs. Configure missing-data handling and separately monitor log-delivery health: a silent agent is not proof that the application is healthy. The alarm evaluates the reported metric over its five-minute period. Delayed log delivery affects detection, and metric filters can occasionally deliver duplicates; this operational signal is not an exactly-once event ledger. An SNS alarm action normally follows a state change rather than sending a fresh message for every additional error.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudWatch agent on on-premises servers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/install-CloudWatch-Agent-on-premise.html); [CloudWatch Logs metric filters](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/MonitoringLogData.html); [CloudWatch alarm behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch_Alarms.html).

diagram_alt: Each matching error adds one to the metric, and the five-minute sum—not CPU or an hourly query—controls the notification.

sources.supports: The unified agent can ship logs from on-premises hosts using configured AWS access and a destination Region.
Metric filters turn matching newly ingested log events in Standard log groups into numerical CloudWatch metrics; they do not process historical events retroactively.
Metric alarms evaluate a statistic over configured periods and can notify SNS when the alarm changes state; current CloudWatch also has other alarm types.

editorial_notes: Preserved answer 4. Made the threshold and ingestion window explicit. Replaced unrelated service distractors with valid monitoring approaches that fail latency, measurement, or custom-code constraints. Avoided claiming that current CloudWatch supports only metric-based alarms.
Root review clarified the metric aggregation period and occasional duplicate delivery documented by CloudWatch, avoiding an unsupported exact ingestion-window claim.
